single.claim: A higher axiological score cannot override an OBLIGATORY-and-feasible option in `govern`; the gradient is confined to ranking *within* the pool that obligation has already forced, so the deontic layer is as un-overridable by utility as the alethic floor is — just at a different layer.
single.title: In govern.mjs, an OBLIGATORY-and-feasible option is immune to axiological override — the gradient ranks only within the obligatory pool, not across it
single.body:
The question requires reading `govern.mjs` and `bridge.mjs` together, because both implement the same structural idea — a higher-priority layer hard-restricts the candidate set before the gradient ever touches it — but at different rungs.

**In `bridge.mjs` (alethic floor):** `consume()` removes infeasible options entirely; a vetoed option gets score `0̲`, which annihilates through `⊗`. The comment is explicit: *"No heuristic utility, however large, can resurrect a vetoed option."* The gradient in `select()` then ranks only the feasible survivors (`B2`). Utility is powerless against the alethic floor.

**In `govern.mjs` (deontic layer):** The identical architectural move is made one rung higher. After the alethic floor filters out infeasible options, `govern` evaluates norms and builds an `obligatoryFeasible` list — options that are both `STATUS.OBLIGATORY` *and* passed `consume()`. The selection pool is then constructed as:

> `const pool = (obligatoryFeasible.length ? obligatoryFeasible : admissible).slice().sort((a, b) => b.utility - a.utility);`

When `obligatoryFeasible` is non-empty, the pool is **exclusively** that set. The `admissible` superset — which includes higher-scoring `STATUS.OPTIONAL` options — is never reached. The axiological sort (`sort((a, b) => b.utility - a.utility)`) operates only *inside* the obligatory pool. A permitted option with utility 1,000,000 sitting in `admissible` but outside `obligatoryFeasible` is simply not in the pool at all.

The governing comment at the top of `govern.mjs` states the design principle directly: *"OBLIGATORY & feasible → FORCED — chosen over any higher-scoring permitted option."* The word "forced" is load-bearing: it describes a hard pool restriction, not a soft penalty or preference weight.

So the ladder enforces two sequential, non-negotiable narrowings before utility ever speaks: first the alethic floor (feasibility), then the deontic layer (obligation). The gradient ranks only what both layers permit. A higher axiological score can influence *which* obligatory option wins if there are several, but it cannot drag a merely-permitted option into contention against an obligatory-and-feasible one.

that's the alethic floor. `consume()` in value.mjs is a boolean gate on the invariant Value structure — it fires before any norm is consulted, before any status is resolved, before govern even builds its `ev` array. when it returns `ok: false`, the option doesn't get a score at all. it gets `S.zero` — the absorbing element — which means `⊗` through any chain returns `0̲` regardless of what's multiplied in. the option is *annihilated*, not recorded, not flagged overridable, just gone.


so: bridge `0̲` = floor, irreversible, absorbing, no record needed because there's nothing to negotiate. govern `deonticallyVetoed` = norm exclusion, reversible in principle, lives in the survivors set, carries override metadata. same word "excluded," completely different ontological category.

confirmed implicated. the operative line is in the govern.mjs header comment:

> `FORBIDDEN (not overridden) → excluded, but RECORDED as overridable (a norm, not a wall).`

that's the categorical marker. deontic exclusion carries three properties the alethic floor cannot carry: it's *recorded* (the `deonticallyVetoed` array exists and is returned in the certificate), it's *attributed* (`by: e.contributors...`), and it's explicitly `overridable: true`. none of those make sense for `S.zero` — you don't record what was annihilated, you don't attribute absorbing-element arithmetic to a norm contributor, and you don't mark a structural impossibility as overridable.

the structural proof is in the sequencing: `const survivors = ev.filter((e) => e.feasible)` runs before `deonticallyVetoed` is even constructed. my rung never sees an alethically-vetoed option. the deontic layer is *definitionally* a layer over the survivors — options that have already cleared `consume()`. so the two exclusions aren't just different in degree; they operate on disjoint populations at different moments in the pipeline. bridge `0̲` removes from the game entirely before norms are consulted. govern `deonticallyVetoed` is a norm verdict on something the game still contains, which is why override is coherent there and incoherent at the alethic floor.

the question is whether two exclusion mechanisms are categorically the same. the axiological gradient doesn't produce either of them. it ranks survivors — options that have already cleared both the alethic floor (`consume()`) and the deontic layer (whatever `govern` didn't mark `FORBIDDEN`). by the time `select()` is called, the gradient receives a set that contains neither `S.zero`-annihilated options nor `deonticallyVetoed` options. both prior rungs have correctly established that those are disjoint populations removed at different pipeline stages for categorically different reasons.

score.mjs's semiring arithmetic is what gives `S.zero` its annihilating property (absorbing element under `⊗`), but *whether* an option is alethically vs. deontically excluded, and *whether* those are the same kind of thing — that's not a question the gradient decides or even observes. the gradient sees admissible options and ranks them. it has no visibility into the mechanism by which excluded options were excluded.

the alethic and deontic owners have correctly handled this question on their own rungs. no ranking involved.
